items.summary_1line: Users often complain that AI assistants such as ChatGPT are getting worse. Some versions do change, but human evaluation leaves a second possibility untested: the people judging may change. We separate the two on Chat...

items.title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge...

items.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. D...

items.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
items.summary_1line: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibiti
items.editor_note: Latest item: shifts from whether scores are trustworthy to whether individual answers are, via a black-box aleatoric/epistemic split.

editorial.tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Oct 27 it ran from continual learning and pruning through Anthropic's Nov 2 provable-inference update and knowledge editing to Nov 10-12 studies questioning what eval scores measure: rater drift, name-anchored recall and corrupted-input shortcuts.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 13: a black-box uncertainty method uses an ensemble of ensembles to split prompt ambiguity from genuine knowledge gaps without the compute cost of Bayesian or deep-ensemble approaches.
editorial.why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but the latest run touches production reliability: scores can survive name removal or shuffled inputs, and black-box uncertainty is the signal an API-only deployment has for deciding when to abstain or escalate.
editorial.take_for_builders: Add perturbed controls to your eval suite (paraphrased entity names, shuffled inputs), and before adopting black-box uncertainty for abstention, measure its extra call cost per request.

open_questions: Does the ensemble-of-ensembles method report how many model calls per prompt it needs, and how that compares with deep ensembles?
Do published unlearning or knowledge-editing methods still pass when probed without explicit entity names, as ShadowBench suggests they may not?
Does the corruption study find LLMs keep accuracy on shuffled or noun-stripped inputs, and does it attribute that to shortcuts or memorised test data?
Do Chatbot Arena or other human-preference leaderboards adjust rankings for the rater drift the Nov 10 study describes?
Does Anthropic publish proving cost or latency figures for zkSNARK-based provable inference?
Does the early-stopping audit identify a method that cuts reasoning tokens without lowering reliability?
